comments.author: @leechumbley5440
comments.text: My head is spinning. I learned many new things. Instagram thrill seekers coming to the wrong castle doesn’t surprise me. But: Trajan wanted the gold mine! Totally new to me and totally passes the plausibility test. The Romanian language coming from Latin’s being the ligua franca of the gold mine work force. Fascinating! I met several persons (before the fall of East Germany’s wall and of the Soviet Union) who in almost ashamed whispers said something about being bought and another obscure whispered reference to Romania – they implied they couldn’t say too much because they would endanger others still ‘over there.‘ It seemed so strange, were they telling the truth? Why so hush-hush and secretive?  Because of your video I now know the truth, West Germany did indeed ‘buy’ them. I appreciate so much finally understanding these interactions. The only 2 times persons physically tried to steal (in Milan, and Missolongi Greece) my wallet were Romas, the second violent and dangerous, along with escaping a threat in Jerez de la Frontiera. So I view them with suspicion. They give the decent persons of their ethnicity a bad name, unfortunately. I didn’t know they had been enslaved half a millenium in Romania. There is so much to mull over from your wonderful presentation. Thank you.

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: That Trajan gold-mine connection is a genuinely striking piece of history - a language surviving as the vernacular of a mining workforce, then outlasting the empire that created the need for it, is a remarkable thread. And the East German "buying" arrangement you'd heard whispered about for years finally getting an explanation must have been its own kind of relief. Thank you for such a rich, curious read of the whole piece.
